title: can, could and (be) able to
subtitle: I can / I could / I was able to
summary: Use can and could to say what is possible or what somebody is able to do, and know when you need (be) able to or managed to instead.

lesson.heading: can: possible, allowed or able
lesson.text: We use **can** to say that something is possible or allowed, or that somebody has the ability to do something. The form is **can + infinitive** (can do / can see etc.). The negative is **can't** (= cannot).

examples.text: We **can see** the lake from our hotel.
'I don't have a pen.' 'You **can use** mine.'
I **can come** and see you tomorrow if you like.
I'm afraid I **can't come** to the party on Friday.

lesson.heading: can or (be) able to?

left.label: can / could
left.text: You can say that somebody *is able to* do something, but can is more usual. Can has only two forms: can (present) and could (past).
examples: Maria **can** speak French, Spanish and English.

right.label: (be) able to
right.text: When you need another form (the perfect, an infinitive, or a form after might / must etc.), can is not possible, so use (be) able to.
examples: I haven't **been able to** sleep recently.
Tom might **be able to** come tomorrow.
Applicants for the job must **be able to** speak two foreign languages.

lesson.note: We are able to see the lake from our hotel is possible, but We can see the lake is more usual.

lesson.heading: could: the past of can
lesson.text: Sometimes **could** is the past of can. We use could especially with the verbs **see, hear, smell, taste, feel, remember** and **understand**. We also use could to say that somebody had the ability to do something, or was allowed to do something.

examples.text: We had a lovely room in the hotel. We **could see** the lake.
As soon as I walked into the room, I **could smell** gas.
I was sitting at the back of the theatre and **couldn't hear** very well.
We were totally free. We **could do** what we wanted.

left.label: could = general ability
left.text: We use could for general ability in the past, and with see, hear etc.
examples: I **could see** them, but not very clearly.
Jack was an excellent tennis player when he was younger. He **could beat** anybody. (= he had the ability)

right.label: was able to / managed to = succeeded once
right.text: To say that somebody succeeded in doing something in a specific situation, we normally use was/were able to or managed to (not could).
examples: The fire spread quickly, but everybody **was able to escape**. (not could escape)
I didn't know where Max was, but I **managed to find** him in the end. (not could find)
Jack and Andy played a match yesterday. Andy played well, but Jack **managed to beat** him. (= he succeeded this time)

lesson.heading: couldn't works in every situation
lesson.text: The negative **couldn't** (could not) is possible in all situations - for general ability in the past and for one specific situation.

examples.text: I looked for Max everywhere, but I **couldn't find** him.
Andy played well, but he **couldn't beat** Jack.

lesson.text: Quick check for the past: a general ability = could; one success in one situation = was able to or managed to; a failure = couldn't, which works for both.

exercises.prompt: Nicole ___ drive, but she doesn't have a car.
exercises.explanation: Present ability: can is the usual form. Be able to is only needed when can is not possible.

exercises.prompt: I used to ___ stand on my head, but I can't do it any more.
exercises.explanation: After used to we need an infinitive, and can has no infinitive form, so: used to be able to.

exercises.prompt: I can't understand Mark. I've never ___ understand him.
exercises.explanation: The present perfect (I've never ...) needs a past participle, so can is not possible: I've never been able to.

exercises.prompt: When Dan was 16, he ___ 100 metres in 11 seconds.
exercises.explanation: A general ability in the past: could run.

exercises.prompt: I don't feel good this morning. I ___ last night.
exercises.explanation: Past and negative: couldn't sleep. Couldn't is possible in every situation.

exercises.prompt: Ask Katherine about your problem. She might ___ help you.
exercises.explanation: After another modal verb (might) we cannot use can or could, so we need be able to.

exercises.prompt: A: Did you finish your work this afternoon? B: Yes, there was nobody to disturb me, so ... Put the words in order to complete B's answer.
exercises.answer: I was able to finish it
exercises.explanation: One success in a specific situation: was able to (not could).

exercises.prompt: A: Did the thief get away? B: Yes. No-one realised what was happening and ... Put the words in order to complete B's answer.
exercises.answer: the thief was able to get away
exercises.explanation: The thief succeeded in one particular situation, so we use was able to.

exercises.statement: The fire spread quickly, but everybody could escape.
exercises.explanation: The fire spread quickly, but everybody was able to escape (or managed to escape). For success in a specific situation, we don't use could.

exercises.statement: My grandfather could speak five languages.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Could is used for general ability in the past.

exercises.prompt: There was a small fire in the kitchen, but fortunately I ___ put it out.
exercises.explanation: Somebody succeeded in doing something in one specific situation: managed to (or was able to), not could.

exercises.prompt: Which word completes each sentence: could, couldn't or managed to?

items.text: The walls were thin and I ___ hear people talking in the next room.
I ran my first marathon recently. It was very hard, but I ___ finish.
My grandmother loved music. She ___ play the piano very well.
We wanted to go to the concert, but we ___ get tickets.
A girl fell into the river, but some people ___ pull her out. She's all right now.
Jessica had hurt her foot and ___ walk very well.
